content: Nitroglycerin, when used in combination with beta-blockers, can lead to additional hypotensive effects in patients with angina pectoris. Beta-blockers reduce the reflex tachycardia caused by nitroglycerin but do not prevent its blood pressure-lowering effects. Close monitoring is required when nitroglycerin is used with medications such as prazosin, propranolol, quinapril, ramipril, sacubitril/valsartan, silodosin, sotalol, spironolactone, telmisartan, terazosin, timolol, tizanidine, torsemide, trandolapril, triamterene, valsartan, or verapamil, as these combinations may result in pharmacodynamic synergism, leading to additive hypotensive effects. The concurrent use of nitroglycerin with PDE5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) is contraindicated due to the risk of severe hypotension caused by additive vasodilation. The interaction between nitroglycerin and PDE5 inhibitors is influenced by the half-life of the PDE5 inhibitor. Nitroglycerin should not be used within a few days of PDE5 inhibitor administration. Intravenous nitroglycerin can reduce the thrombolytic effect of tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) by lowering plasma levels of t-PA. Caution is advised when nitroglycerin is co-administered with t-PA therapy. Similarly, nitroglycerin may decrease the effects of reteplase and tenecteplase. Nitroglycerin can cause dose-related headaches, which may be severe, although tolerance to these headaches can develop over time. Other adverse effects include dizziness, lightheadedness, nausea, vomiting, hypotension (including orthostatic hypotension), flushing, allergic reactions, and application site reactions such as drug rash or exfoliative dermatitis. Methemoglobinemia may occur, particularly in cases of overdose. Patients with hypersensitivity to nitroglycerin or its excipients, or those with idiosyncratic reactions to other organic nitrates, should avoid its use. Nitroglycerin is contraindicated in patients with severe anemia, increased intracranial pressure (e.g., head trauma, cerebral hemorrhage), or inadequate cerebral circulation. It should also be avoided in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to the risk of exacerbating the condition. Caution is advised when nitroglycerin is used in patients with existing cardiovascular disorders, blood volume depletion, hypotension, cardiomyopathies, congestive heart failure (CHF), acute myocardial infarction (MI), or poor cardiac function. Nitroglycerin may cause venous and arterial dilation, reducing venous blood return to the heart, arterial vascular resistance, and systolic pressure. Co-administration with aspirin may increase nitroglycerin's maximum serum concentration and area under the curve (AUC). Alcohol can enhance nitroglycerin's vasodilating effects. Additive hypotensive effects may occur when nitroglycerin is used with nitric oxide donors (e.g., long-acting nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate, amyl nitrite, butyl nitrite), antihypertensive drugs, beta-adrenergic blockers, or calcium channel blockers. Marked orthostatic hypotension has been reported with the concomitant use of calcium channel blockers and organic nitrates. Nitroglycerin is classified as Pregnancy Category C. There is no evidence of fetal risk in controlled studies in pregnant women, but caution is advised. It is unknown whether nitroglycerin is distributed in breast milk, so caution should be exercised during lactation.
